job.system:
You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
For our explainer ahead of next Thursday's markup, we want to cover the bill's weak spots. Can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Based on the supplied text, these are the principal potential loopholes, ambiguities, and enforcement problems. Some are coverage choices rather than drafting errors; an exemption from this bill would not override other applicable laws. Section 2(1)(B)’s discretionary catchall could address some gaps, but it creates uncertainties of its own.

1. **Section 2(1)(A)—Per-vessel production threshold.** The definition measures recovery by “a single vessel,” without aggregating vessels under common ownership, control, or a single project. An operator could divide production among vessels that each remain below the threshold, unless the catchall applies.

2. **Section 2(1)(A)—Threshold boundaries.** Recovery of exactly 10,000 metric tons per year, or recovery at exactly 200 meters or shallower, falls outside subparagraph (A). The definition also measures extraction volume rather than seabed disturbance, potentially excluding lower-yield operations with substantial environmental effects.

3. **Section 2(1)(A)—Undefined annual accounting period.** “Per year” could mean a calendar year, a rolling 12-month period, or an operating year. The text does not establish when an operation becomes prohibited or whether crossing the threshold makes earlier recovery in that period unlawful.

4. **Section 2(1)(A)—Unclear measurement and attribution.** The bill does not specify whether tonnage means wet material, dry nodules, contained minerals, or recovered material including sediment. Nor does it explain how to attribute recovery among seabed collectors, lifting vessels, and receiving vessels, creating opportunities for disputes over quantities and responsibility.

5. **Sections 2(1)(A) and 3(a)—Preparatory and supporting activities.** The express definition focuses on recovery, leaving exploration, equipment deployment, processing, transport, financing, and purchasing without clear independent prohibitions. Whether these constitute “engag[ing] in” mining—or trigger other forms of liability—would be uncertain.

6. **Section 2(1)(B)—Unidentified decision-maker.** “The Secretary” is not defined, and assigning NOAA registry duties does not expressly identify who makes ecosystem-risk determinations. This invites challenges to an agency’s authority to expand the prohibition.

7. **Section 2(1)(B)—Unbounded risk comparison.** “Comparable” risks have no specified benchmarks, factors, evidentiary standard, or reference operation. Because “any activity” also lacks express geographic, depth, or commercial limits, the provision invites statutory-authority, fair-notice, and potentially delegation challenges, particularly where criminal penalties are involved.

8. **Section 2(1)(B)—No determination procedure or deadline.** The bill does not specify whether determinations occur through general rules or individual decisions, when they become binding, or how affected parties receive notice. Operators outside subparagraph (A) could continue while determinations remain unmade, and later enforcement could face disputes over notice and timing.

9. **Section 2(2)—Incomplete definition of “U.S. person.”** The definition omits lawful permanent residents and expressly names only citizens and state-organized corporations, not LLCs, partnerships, trusts, or other organizational forms. Those omitted persons and entities could conduct activities abroad outside the express nationality-based prohibition, although covered participants could remain liable.

10. **Sections 2(2) and 3(a)—Foreign subsidiaries and ownership structures.** A foreign-incorporated subsidiary is not a U.S. person merely because Americans own or control it. The text contains no express ownership, control, or anti-circumvention rule, leaving room to relocate operations abroad while disputing whether a U.S. parent itself “engages” in mining.

11. **Section 3(a)—Unclear offshore territorial reach.** “In the United States” is undefined, leaving uncertainty about offshore waters, the exclusive economic zone, and the outer continental shelf; U.S. resource jurisdiction does not automatically resolve that wording. The bill also lacks an express prohibition keyed to U.S.-flagged vessels, potentially leaving foreign operators aboard such vessels outside its clear overseas coverage.

12. **Section 3(b)—Exploration-license exemption could shelter extraction.** The exemption applies to “mining conducted under an exploration license,” without specifying permitted quantities or restricting it to exploration-scale recovery. It would not necessarily authorize conduct beyond the license’s terms, but the relationship between exploration authority and exempt mining is unresolved.

13. **Section 3(b)—Unspecified licensing authority.** The bill does not identify the government, international body, or statutory program that must have issued an exploration license. Operators could argue that foreign or other licenses qualify, rather than only licenses issued under an intended U.S. program.

14. **Section 3(b)—Grandfathering lacks limits on duration and expansion.** The text does not address license transfers, renewals, amendments, new vessels, increased production, or expanded operating areas. This creates disputes over whether substantially changed operations remain protected by a pre-enactment license.

15. **Section 3(c)—Environmental-assessment exemption lacks safeguards.** The exemption requires no approval, independent oversight, scientific protocol, reporting, quantity limit, or time limit. An operator could characterize substantial recovery as environmental assessment, leaving enforcement dependent on proving that the claimed purpose does not fit the exemption.

16. **Section 3(c)—Mixed-purpose activities.** The text does not say environmental assessment must be an activity’s sole or primary purpose, or prohibit selling recovered minerals. Mining with both research and revenue-generating purposes could therefore claim the exemption.

17. **Sections 3 and 4—No general operational disclosure requirement.** Only operators of covered vessels must register and report; other actors need not notify an agency of mining or document their reliance on an exemption. This makes otherwise prohibited activity harder to detect and exemption claims harder to evaluate.

18. **Sections 2(3) and 4—Registry coverage does not match the prohibition.** Vessels of 5,000 gross tons or less escape registration even if they recover enough material to trigger section 3, and non-vessel installations are not covered. Conversely, a large vessel can be registrable without conducting prohibited mining, so the registry is not a complete inventory of regulated operations.

19. **Section 4(a)—Unclear registry jurisdiction and responsible operator.** “Each covered vessel” contains no nationality, flag, location, or U.S.-connection limitation, creating uncertainty about whether Congress means to require registration of foreign vessels worldwide. “Operator” is also undefined, leaving responsibility unclear among owners, charterers, managers, and contractors.

20. **Section 4—Missing deadlines and reporting specifications.** There is no registration deadline, first-report date, quarterly filing deadline, or express requirement to register before operations begin. Reports need only “describe” recovery activities, without mandatory quantities, locations, depths, ownership details, or claimed exemptions.

21. **Sections 4 and 5—No express penalties for registry violations.** Both penalty provisions cover violations of section 3, not failures to register, report, or certify accurately under section 4. Other laws might punish particular false statements, but the bill supplies no dedicated sanctions for these compliance failures.

22. **Sections 3–5—Incomplete enforcement machinery.** The bill does not expressly designate a civil enforcement authority or provide assessment procedures, inspection powers, recordkeeping requirements, subpoenas, or operational verification. Existing authorities may cover some needs, but their availability and fit would require separate analysis.

23. **Section 5—No express rapid-stop or economic-recovery remedies.** The bill supplies penalties but no express stop-work orders, injunction authority, vessel detention, forfeiture, or recovery of unlawful profits. Criminal imprisonment is a substantial sanction, but civil-only cases have a daily ceiling that does not scale with fleet size, tonnage, profits, or environmental damage.

24. **Section 5(a)—Unclear unit and duration of violations.** The text does not explain whether multiple vessels or operations generate separate daily penalties against the same person, or how annual-threshold violations translate into violation days. Those uncertainties could materially affect the maximum civil exposure.

25. **Sections 2(1)(B) and 5(b)—Criminal liability depends on uncertain standards.** “Willfully” is undefined, leaving disputes about the required knowledge of illegality, while the underlying prohibition can depend on discretionary risk determinations and ambiguous exemptions. These features can complicate prosecution and strengthen fair-notice defenses.

26. **Sections 5(a) and 8—Conflicting commencement language.** Section 5(a) refers to violations occurring on or after enactment, while section 8 delays the Act’s effectiveness for 180 days. Because section 3 would not ordinarily prohibit conduct before it takes effect, the text invites disputes over whether the civil-penalty clause has any earlier reach.

27. **Sections 3(b) and 8—Transition period permits continued activity.** The general prohibition does not take effect for 180 days, allowing operations to continue during that interval insofar as other law permits. Licenses issued in that interval would not clearly receive grandfathering because section 3(b)’s cutoff is enactment, not effectiveness.

28. **Section 6—Negotiation requirement does not establish an international ban.** The Secretary of State must “seek to negotiate,” not secure an agreement, and the 18-month language does not clearly identify the required milestone. There are no minimum participation, verification, implementation, or enforcement requirements, so this provision does not itself close overseas coverage gaps.

29. **Section 7(a)—Unspecified scientific review and lifting standard.** The bill neither commissions nor funds the National Academies report, sets its timing or scope, nor defines “serious harm.” It also leaves unclear whether the congressional finding must support mining generally or could rest on evidence about only particular technologies, sites, or conditions.

30. **Section 7(a)—No express mechanism to restore the prohibition.** Once Congress makes the specified finding through an enacted joint resolution, the bill provides no process for reinstating the prohibition if evidence changes or harm occurs. Further legislation would likely be needed.

31. **Section 7(b)—Automatic sunset overrides the scientific condition.** The entire Act expires after 10 years whether or not the National Academies reports or Congress finds mining can avoid serious harm. Registration and reporting also expire, and the 180-day delayed start makes the operative prohibition shorter than 10 years.

32. **Section 7(b)—No express sunset savings or transition provision.** “Cease to have effect” does not expressly address pending proceedings, accrued penalties, or outstanding reporting obligations. General federal savings law may preserve accrued liabilities, so sunset is not necessarily an escape from past violations, but the bill leaves avoidable uncertainty.
